newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-GERMANS OFFER TALKS WITH ENGLAND ON WORLD CUP ROW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GERMANS OFFER TALKS WITH ENGLAND ON WORLD CUP ROW.

text.p: German soccer boss Egidius Braun said on Friday he was ready to talk to English officials about finding a solution to their rival bids for the 2006 World Cup.
He also said there had been a previous, unofficial understanding between the two countries that England would support Germany's bid.
Braun's offer came three days after national team coach Berti Vogts called on the English Football Association (F.A.) to scrap their bid, saying it had not kept its word to stay out of the race.
Braun adopted a more diplomatic approach.

"If the English came to me I would be prepared to talk to them any day of the week," he said in an interview. "Two bids from Europe won't work because the vote will be split and a European country won't get it."

World governing body FIFA will not decide on the venue for the finals until the year 2000. But the Germans are keen to avoid the kind of expensive, bitter campaigning which embroiled Japan and South Korea in a battle to stage the 2002 World Cup.
The tournament was eventually shared between the two countries but this is not an option in the case of England and Germany and the two countries are presently on course for a battle.
Braun disclosed how the Germans, who launched their bid in 1993 -- three years before England -- had come to believe they would get the full backing of the English F.A..

Braun said he had been a major supporter of England in their efforts to end the suspension of English clubs from European competition and their campaign to host last year's European championship finals.

The German soccer federation (DFB) chief said he had at no time carried out detailed negotiations with close friend and former English chief Bert Millichip in which the Germans expected anything in return for its support.
But it appears it was understood that there would be mutual back-scratching between the two officials which was never discussed at any official meeting or ever recorded in minutes.
Braun said it was known throughout Europe that Germany was bidding for the tournament.

"I never asked for anything in return but we both patted each other on the shoulder and said 'I'll do it'," Braun said. "You know some of the most important things are not in the minutes (of a meeting)."
"When it was later asked if any other European country was interested in staging the finals, no other country came forward. The situation was quite clear."

Braun said he had a huge amount of respect for Millichip. The two men have clearly still got a very good relationship. They both travelled together to a meeting of the world governing body FIFA this week, chatting happily on the plane.
The German boss said he felt the English bid had become a political issue with former Conservative Prime Minister John Major keen to back it.
"I get the impression that Major was interested in making it an issue," Braun said. "He was successful in that."
Braun said he was very disappointed by England's attitude and he would not himself be ready to initiate talks with the F.A..
"Of all the countries, we expected to get their support," he said. "We are disappointed."

The Germans believe the English have a reputation for fair play but have let themselves down on this issue. On Tuesday Vogts called on new prime minister Tony Blair to tell the F.A. to withdraw their bid.
